questions.q: What does it mean, concretely, to treat a platform as a product rather than a mandate?
options: The platform team applies product-management discipline — user research, a prioritized roadmap, and iteration driven by feedback — to the internal platform
The platform team sells the platform externally as a paid SaaS offering
The platform team stops accepting any requests from other teams
The platform team ships whatever features leadership decides, with no user research
questions.explain: Platform as a product means applying the same discipline a company uses for an external product — understanding users, maintaining a roadmap, shipping iteratively, and acting on feedback — pointed inward at the platform's own users.

questions.q: Who are the platform team's customers, in this operating model?
options: External paying clients of the company
The company's board of directors
The finance department's budget owners
The internal developers and stream-aligned teams who actually use the platform to build and ship software
questions.explain: In the platform-as-a-product model, the internal engineers who consume the platform are its real customers — the people whose needs determine whether the platform is actually succeeding.

questions.q: What failure mode does this lesson describe when a platform is mandatory but not built with product thinking?
options: The platform becomes too inexpensive to operate
The platform launches too slowly due to excessive user research
Usage dashboards can look healthy while teams quietly build shadow infrastructure or route around the platform because it doesn't meet their real needs
The platform has too many feedback channels for developers to use
questions.explain: A mandate doesn't guarantee real adoption. Teams that aren't well served by the platform build workarounds instead — the mandate stays technically in force while practical usage quietly collapses.

questions.q: What does Team Topologies' X-as-a-Service interaction mode require of a platform team that collaboration mode doesn't?
options: No interaction at all between the platform team and the teams it serves
A self-service interface good enough that consuming teams rarely need to escalate to a human on the platform team
The platform team actively co-writes every feature alongside each consuming team
The platform team unblocks unrelated technical debt for every team it serves
questions.explain: X-as-a-Service means the platform exposes a well-defined interface — an API, template, or portal — that teams consume directly. That only works if the interface itself is good enough to need minimal ongoing hand-holding.

questions.q: Which practice does this lesson associate with genuinely running a platform like a product?
options: Maintaining feedback channels that visibly change what the platform team builds next, not ones that collect input and act on nothing
Freezing the platform's roadmap permanently once it first ships
Removing documentation to encourage teams to experiment on their own
Avoiding direct contact with the developers who actually use the platform
questions.explain: A feedback loop that never changes outcomes isn't real feedback, it's theater. Product thinking requires that developer input actually reshapes the roadmap.
